Now, an inside video from Anirudh and Kavya's wedding festivities is making rounds on the internet. Rajinikanth appears to have stolen the spotlight as he is seen enjoying the celebrations and dancing to some of Anirudh's popular songs. The video has caught the attention of fans, who are enjoying this special moment from the wedding.
Rajinikanth dances to Anirudh's songs at the wedding
In the viral video, Rajinikanth is seen dancing to songs from Petta and Vettaiyan, both of which feature music composed by Anirudh. The actor appears to be in a cheerful mood as he joins the celebrations and enjoys the music.
Rajinikanth shares a close family connection with the composer. He is married to Anirudh's aunt, Latha, and attended the wedding along with his elder daughter, Aishwarya. The video has given fans a glimpse of the relaxed and celebratory atmosphere at the couple's wedding.
Anirudh Ravichander - Kavya Maran wedding pictures
Anirudh also shared a series of pictures with Kavya from their wedding ceremony. He captioned the post, “My once in a lifetime, for a lifetime (sic).” The couple chose November 11, an 11:11 date, for their wedding.
Anirudh and Kavya to host grand reception - Venue, date and guest list
Following their intimate wedding in Greece, Anirudh and Kavya are reportedly preparing for a grand reception on November 21. The couple's family have invited Telangana Chief Minister Revanth Reddy and his family to the celebrations.
Several film personalities are also expected to attend the reception. Shah Rukh Khan, Dhanush, Allu Arjun, Nayanthara, Sivakarthikeyan and his wife Aarthi, AR Rahman, Ajith Kumar and director Nelson Dilipkumar are among those reportedly invited.
Meanwhile, on the work front, Rajinikanth was last seen in Jailer 2. Now, he is currently shooting for Dharman, directed by Aswath Marimuthu. The film also features Ram Pothineni, Rashii Khanna, Nayanthara and Sreeleela in key roles.

Neminatha (Devanagari: नेमिनाथ) (Sanskrit: नेमिनाथः), also known as Nemi and Ariṣṭanemi (Devanagari: अरिष्टनेमि), is the 22nd tirthankara of Jainism in the present cosmic age (Avasarpini). Along with Mahavira, Pārśvanātha and Rishabhanatha, he is one of the most devotionally revered tirthankaras within the Jain tradition. While his physical historical existence is debated by modern scholars, Indologists such as Damodar Dharmananda Kosambi connect him to the sage Ghora Angirasa from the Vedic Chandogya Upanishad, who instructed Krishna in the virtues of absolute nonviolence (ahimsa). Jain tradition calculates that Neminatha lived tens of thousands of years before the 23rd tirthankara, Pārśvanātha; general accounts cite a gap of 84,000 years, while specific texts like Hemachandra's Trishashtishalakapurusha Charitra calculate the gap at 81,000 years.
In Jain theology and literature, Neminatha is celebrated as a contemporary and cousin of the Hindu deity Krishna, born into the Yadu dynasty in the city of Śaurīpura. His parents are named as Samudravijaya and Shivadevi Jain epics, such as the Harivamsa Purana, utilize the dynamic between the two cousins to contrast Krishna's violent, worldly conquests with Neminatha's supreme spiritual asceticism. Traditional accounts mention his date of birth as the fifth day of Shravan Shukla of the Jain calendar.
Neminatha's defining mythological narrative centers on his profound compassion. Jain tradition holds that upon hearing the cries of animals penned for slaughter at his wedding feast, he immediately renounced his betrothed, Rajmati, his royal lineage, and all worldly attachments (aparigraha). He retreated to Mount Girnar in the Saurashtra region of modern-day Gujarat, where he became an Jain monk and ultimately attained omniscience (Kevala Jnana) and liberation (moksha).
Due to his exclusive geographical association with his ascetic life and liberation, Mount Girnar evolved into one of the most prominent and historically contested Jain pilgrimage sites on the Indian subcontinent. In Jain iconography, Neminatha is traditionally identified by a dark-bluish complexion and the conch shell (shankha) emblem. He is frequently depicted alongside his dedicated guardian deities, the Yaksha Gomedha (or Sarvanha) and the highly venerated Yakshi Ambika.
The name Neminatha consists of two Sanskrit words, Nemi which means "rim, felly of a wheel" or alternatively "thunderbolt",[4] and natha which means "lord, patron, protector".[5]
According to the 9th-10th century CE Jain text Uttarapurana of Jinasena (Digambara monk), as well as the explanation of Hemachandra (11th century CE Śvetāmbara monk), it was the ancient Indian deity Indra who named the 22nd tirthankara as Neminatha, because he viewed the Jina as the "rim of the wheel of dharma".[6]

SOURCE inviteeq.com (Neminath story: why the groom turned back from his own baraat):
In the Jain tradition, Prince Neminath, the 22nd Tirthankara, was on his way to marry Princess Rajul when he heard the cries of animals and birds penned up for the wedding feast. Moved by compassion, he had them freed, turned his chariot back, renounced the world and practised austerities on Mount Girnar. Rajul took diksha too.
The sehra is tied, the baraat is dressed in its best, the drums are going, and at a palace window the bride is waiting. Then the groom’s chariot turns round and leaves. It sounds like the plot of a film. In the Jain tradition it is one of the best-loved stories there is, and part of the reason a Jain wedding feast looks the way it does.
Who was Neminath?
Neminath, also called Arishtanemi, is the 22nd of the 24 Tirthankaras of Jainism. A Tirthankara, literally a ford-maker, is a teacher who has crossed the stream of rebirth and shows others the way across. In the Jain tellings, Neminath was a prince of the Yadavas, the son of King Samudravijaya, and so a cousin of Krishna. His emblem is the conch, the shankh.
His marriage was arranged with Princess Rajul, also called Rajimati, the daughter of King Ugrasena. Her home is popularly placed at Junagadh in Gujarat, near Mount Girnar.
The baraat that turned back
The wedding procession set out for Rajul’s door, with Neminath riding in his chariot. On the way he heard cries, and saw animals and birds shut in pens and cages beside the road. His charioteer told him they were meant for the wedding feast.
Filled with karuna, compassion, Neminath had every pen opened and every animal and bird set free. Then he turned his chariot round, away from the wedding.
Karuna se bhare Neminath ne saare baade khulwa diye, aur rath mod liya. Filled with compassion, Neminath had every pen opened, and turned his chariot back.
Girnar, and Rajul’s diksha
Neminath renounced the world and went to Mount Girnar to practise austerities. Jains hold that it was on Girnar that he attained kevala jnana, perfect knowledge, and later moksha, liberation from rebirth, and the mountain is a place of Jain pilgrimage.
Rajul, too, took diksha, initiation into the life of a renunciant, and followed his path as a nun.
The story is told in the Svetambara scriptures, in the twenty-second chapter of the Uttaradhyayana Sutra and in the Kalpa Sutra’s lives of the Jinas, and among Digambaras in Jinasena’s Harivamsha Purana. The tellings differ in some details, such as who arranged the feast and Krishna’s part in it, but they share this core.
Ahimsa, karuna and the wedding feast
Ahimsa, non-violence, and karuna, compassion, are at the heart of Jainism, and Neminath turning back from his own wedding is often told as a picture of both. That is also part of why a Jain wedding feast is purely vegetarian. Many Jain families go further and leave out onion, garlic and root vegetables, though practice varies from home to home.
None of this makes a Jain wedding any less joyful. A wedding is a celebration, and compassion is part of it too. The feast is still a feast, as any guest will tell you.
